title: Correlation Isn't Causation
objective: After this level you can explain why two things rising and falling together doesn't show that one causes the other.
summary: Two things can rise and fall together without one causing the other. Messerli's 2012 chocolate and Nobel prizes note made the point with a straight face.

cards.headline: Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel prizes. Time for dessert?
cards.body: That was the finding of a short note in a leading medical journal in 2012, and the numbers were real. Switzerland topped both lists. Before you unwrap a second bar in the name of science, ask what a pattern like that can actually show.

cards.headline: Going together versus causing
cards.body: A correlation describes how two things vary together: how strongly, and in which direction. Causation is different: one event is the result of the other. Here's the catch. If A really causes B, the two will be correlated. But a correlation on its own is usually weak evidence that one thing causes the other.

cards.headline: The chocolate note
cards.body: Franz Messerli compared chocolate eaten per person with Nobel laureates per 10 million people in 23 countries and found a close correlation. Then he wrote the key line himself: a correlation between X and Y doesn't prove causation. It means X influences Y, Y influences X, or both are influenced by something underneath. Chocolate might sharpen minds. Or not.

cards.headline: A joke with a point
cards.body: The note ran in the journal's Occasional Notes section, a home for lighter pieces, and it was meant as a friendly reminder that over-reading correlations leads to wrong claims. Some journalists still treated the respected journal as a sign of quality. The lesson isn't that chocolate is useless. It's that "these go together" and "this causes that" are two different claims.

mascot.line: Keep this: "goes together" and "causes" are two different claims. Check which one you've actually been shown.

cards.headline: Correlation: understood
learned: A correlation: two things vary together
Causation: one results from the other
Correlation alone is weak evidence of cause
Messerli's chocolate note made the point

questions.prompt: Franz Messerli's 2012 note linked countries' chocolate eating to their _____.

options.label: rates of heart disease
options.rationale: Not in this note: the comparison was with Nobel prizes.

options.label: average school grades
options.rationale: He used Nobel laureates, not school grades.

questions.explanation: He compared chocolate eaten per person with Nobel laureates per 10 million people in 23 countries.

questions.prompt: Match each term with its description.

pairs.right: One event is the result of the other

questions.explanation: A correlation describes how two things vary together. Causation means one event is the result of the other. The chocolate note ran in Occasional Notes, a home for lighter pieces.

questions.prompt: "Chocolate-loving countries win more Nobels, so chocolate must sharpen minds." What is the conclusion?

options.label: That chocolate-loving countries win more Nobels
options.rationale: That's the premise: the reason offered.

options.label: That Nobel prizes measure intelligence
options.rationale: An unstated assumption, not the conclusion.

options.label: That Switzerland eats the most chocolate
options.rationale: Not stated in this argument at all.

questions.explanation: The correlation is the premise; the causal claim is the conclusion drawn from it, and the weak step.
